Subject: Token flow inventory for dedicated sizing

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for taking time last week. As we discussed, Aurora is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for our customer-facing clinical assistant (real-time chat) and a nightly batch summarization pipeline. To move forward with sizing we put together a short token/profile inventory (attached) and a couple of sample prompts (prompt_samples.pdf). High-level notes: 

- Peak concurrent users (chat sessions): ~1,200 during business hours (08:00-18:00 PT) with a weekly peak day.
- Average prompt length: 45 tokens; median response length: 220 tokens. 10% of responses exceed 1,000 tokens (long report generation).
- Summarization batch: 20k documents overnight; average doc 1,800 tokens; we want batch throughput to complete within a 6 hour window.
- Latency sensitivity for chat: p95 end-to-end <= 400ms for short queries, p99 <= 1.5s for typical flows. Longer report generation can be async.

We'd like a preliminary recommended GPU mix, oversubscription guidance, and any constraints you need (e.g., quantization limits for the long-tail requests). Can you confirm what additional fields you need in the CSV?

Attaching: aurora_token_profile.csv, prompt_samples.pdf

Thanks,
Alice Nguyen
Director of Product
Aurora Health

From: tessa_morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.com>

Hi Alice — thanks for the files, this is a great start. Quick clarifying questions so we can size conservatively before a hands-on profiling workshop: 

1) Can you split the peak concurrency by endpoint type (chat short queries vs long report generation) for the business-hour peak? Even rough percents help (e.g., 80/20).
2) For the 10% long responses, are they generated synchronously in the same request as a chat, or via an async job?
3) For the batch job, are documents processed as independent calls (one request per doc) or bundled into multi-document prompts?
4) Can you confirm expected RPS bursts (e.g., sustained 5m averages vs 1m spikes) and whether any SLAs require headroom for sudden spikes (on-call pages)?

We'll prepare a conservative GPU-mix sketch (GPU SKUs, expected concurrent sessions per GPU, and an oversubscription guardrail). If you can send a simple CSV with columns: endpoint, pct_of_traffic, avg_prompt_tokens, avg_response_tokens, 95th_response_tokens, synchronous_async, typical_batch_size — that would be ideal.

Also looping in Marissa and Ben to suggest initial quantization/latency tradeoffs and to plan a light profiling run.

Best,
Tessa Morgan
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
From: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Date: Mon, 30 Jul 2028 11:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Token flow inventory for dedicated sizing

Quick internal note — for Aurora: given 1,200 peak concurrent sessions with a 10% long-tail, I would initially target a mix of 8 x A100-80GB equiv for synchronous chat capacity + a 2 x A100 (or 4 x L4) pool dedicated to long report jobs (or route long reports to a separate queue with different batching). Oversubscription guidance: 1.5x for short-chat optimized models, no >1.0x for long report generation unless batched.

We should recommend they profile two model variants: one standard 70B quantized path for chat, and a 13B high-throughput path for short queries with aggressive quantization. Ask them for p95 token processing times if they have any in-house traces.

I'll draft a short SOW-style checklist for the capacity workshop (profiling steps, required sample sizes, test harness).

— Marissa
VP, Pre-Sales Solutions

From: ben_carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Token flow inventory for dedicated sizing

Thanks for the breakdown, Alice — this is actionable. Preliminary sizing notes (ballpark, subject to profiling):

- Short chat footprint: assume 120 tokens total per interaction (prompt+resp) => ~80 requests/sec sustained at 1,200 concurrent with avg think-time factored. For short-chat optimized 13B quantized variant on L4-type nodes, expect ~250 concurrent sessions per node at p95 latency target; recommend 5 L4 nodes (with 1.5x oversubscription = config for ~375 effective concurrent).
- Long synchronous reports: heavy token processors — recommend routing to A100-80GB class nodes; each A100 can handle ~6 long-report concurrent sessions (depending on model size). For 10% of 1,200 peak = 120 concurrent long jobs => need ~20 A100 equivalents (we can layer batching/async to reduce this).
- Batch summarization: 20k docs / 6h => ~930 docs/hour => ~15 docs/minute; with batching (50-doc jobs) this fits into a small dedicated batch pool of 4 x A100 equivalents for throughput and headroom.

Risks/notes: 95th token-processing times will shift these numbers; quantization can help short-chat but may degrade clinical-quality outputs — need to flag for their clinical reviewers. Also call out the 1m spike to 2.4x baseline; recommend configuring burst capacity (on-demand nodes or spillover to hosted) rather than oversubscribing beyond 1.5x.

Next steps: 1) Schedule a 90-minute profiling workshop (we'll run sample requests against a short/long model variant). 2) Exchange a small profiling harness (we'll send a JAR + curl examples). 3) Draft an initial resource estimate and cost model for procurement.

— Ben Carter
Principal Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference
